issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For physical abuse by a romantic partner, the threat profile is centered on generalized danger from strangers, while the appraisals are centered on bodily damage/shame and permanent emotional change. This is not impossible, but as the only represented components it is clinically hard to integrate into a single coherent profile of partner abuse without any partner-specific or trauma-linked threat content.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active links are between Negative Appraisals and Threat, so these two nodes should strongly cohere. Here the negative appraisals imply consequences focused on the body and self after intimate physical abuse, but the threat item 'threat from strangers approaching me' points to a different danger representation that is not reflected in the appraisals. That weakens the expected tight appraisal-threat coupling.

vignette:
Eighty-year-old Malia still remembers the weight of his hand on her shoulder, the way it would tighten just before he shoved her into the kitchen counter. For thirty years, she had been a welder—strong, steady, able to hold a torch steady for hours—but none of that strength had helped her when her husband’s temper flared. The worst night had been a Tuesday, after she’d stayed late finishing a repair job. He accused her of lying about where she’d been, and when she tried to walk past him to the bedroom, he grabbed her arm and slammed her against the doorframe. She felt something pop in her lower back, a sharp, lasting pain that never fully went away. He was dead now, six years gone, but the damage he’d done to her body remained.

Malia has come to believe that her body has been permanently damaged by what happened. She feels it every morning when she tries to get out of bed—the stiffness in her spine, the ache that radiates down her left leg. She tells herself that her body is no longer trustworthy, that it can betray her without warning, and this belief has made her hypervigilant. She now sleeps in fits, waking several times a night to check that the front door is locked, that the windows are secure, that no one has entered the house while she was unconscious. She is alert at home in a way she never was before, scanning the hallway from her armchair, listening for footsteps that aren’t there. She has come to feel that her body’s fragility means she must be constantly watchful, because if her body fails her, no one else will protect her.

Her heightened watchfulness, in turn, only deepens her sense that something is wrong with her. The more she checks and scans, the more she feels that her body is unreliable—that it is reacting to threats that aren’t there, that it is keeping her trapped in a state of alarm she cannot control. She has told her daughter that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again, that the person she was before the abuse is gone. She feels hollowed out, as though the fear has burned away everything else. 

At work, Malia had always been known for her steady hands and calm demeanor, but now she finds herself flinching when a coworker touches her shoulder unexpectedly. She has started avoiding the break room during lunch, because the sound of raised voices from the television makes her chest tighten. She retired early, unable to tolerate the noise and the closeness of the workshop floor. At home, her husband—her second husband, a gentle man who never raises his voice—doesn’t understand why she insists on locking every door twice, why she sleeps with the light on. She cannot explain it to him. She only knows that her body feels like a broken instrument, and that she must keep watch over it constantly.

What finally brought her to seek help was a night last month when she woke up screaming, certain that someone was standing over her bed. Her husband found her in the corner of the bedroom, her back pressed against the wall, her hands shaking. She is afraid that she is losing her mind, that the fear will never stop. She hopes, quietly, that someone can help her learn to trust her own body again—or at least to sleep through the night.
